cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: 1234 rendered as Thai text with a Baht suffix
cases.expected: หนึ่งพันสองร้อยสามสิบสี่บาทถ้วน
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as the Thai string for "one thousand two hundred thirty four Baht", transcribed here character for character from the page: หนึ่ง (one) พัน (thousand) สอง (two) ร้อย (hundred) สาม (three) สิบ (ten) สี่ (four) บาท (Baht) ถ้วน (exactly). The documented output is a 31-character Thai string

cases.description: The result is a text value, not a number
cases.expected_note: Excel documents BAHTTEXT as converting "a number to Thai text", so the result is a text value and ISTEXT is TRUE. This case survives any locale-dependent difference in the Baht wording, unlike the exact-string case above

Excel documents the single argument as "A number you want to convert to text, or a reference to a cell containing a number, or a formula that evaluates to a number"; non-numeric text is the wrong argument type, which is Excel's documented #VALUE! case
